prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall state and Z2 topological insulators, and its first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: Topological insulators are the one candidate on which the committee is broadly aligned: seven of eight members place B013 in their top three, and I do too. The physics is a genuine change in how electronic matter is classified. A Z2 invariant protected by time-reversal symmetry was predicted (Kane and Mele), and the quantum spin Hall edge channels were then seen in HgTe wells by Molenkamp's group, so prediction and decisive measurement sit in the same story. Many independent groups have since reproduced it in transport and photoemission across several material families, so the independent-confirmation test I apply is passed and the result is more than a decade old. I moved from my opening first choice, IceCube, because the attribution there is weaker (one credited name for a very large collaboration with earlier pioneers) while B013 has a workable, widely shared three-person core. The Kane, Mele, Molenkamp trio is proposed by seven of the eight openings, including mine. As Chair I would also rather build on that convergence than defend a personal preference for an instrument-driven discovery.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution and overlap, not maturity. Four people are credited but only three seats exist, and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal, which directly enabled the Molenkamp experiment, is outside the credited names, so the trio can look like it skips a link in the chain. Leaving out Hasan means the three-dimensional topological insulator discovery is not recognised, and the committee has to say whether the 2D quantum spin Hall effect is a fair and complete scope for the citation. The 2016 prize on topological phases and phase transitions will also lead some to ask whether a second topological prize is too close. The 2016 prize addressed topological phase transitions and the quantum Hall-type phases, whereas this one is about time-reversal-protected band topology, but the committee should be able to state that difference plainly. Finally, condensed matter is outside my expertise, so I am relying on colleagues for the finer points of who did what first.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B013 first but would credit Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, leaving out Mele, because Hasan's ARPES work established the 3D topological insulator experimentally.
responses.response: I take the Hasan argument seriously, since the 3D materials work is what turned the idea into a broad materials field and gave ARPES confirmation. But I cannot support dropping Mele. He co-authored the Z2 papers with Kane, and a prize for the quantum spin Hall prediction without him would be hard to defend. Seven of eight openings, including mine, chose Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. I would keep the citation tied to the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 classification, where theory and first experiment are clean. I would also ask you to say whether you think the 3D branch is a separate achievement that deserves its own part rather than a swap of one name. With a three-person limit I do not see room for that in this configuration.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B013 first as a clean general mechanism, spin-orbit coupling plus time-reversal symmetry giving a Z2 classification, and proposes two theorists and the first experimentalist, noting the awkward absence of BHZ.
responses.response: I agree with the structure of your proposal and with your point that Kane and Mele turned a messy band-structure problem into a rigorous invariant, which is the part of the credit I would call most decisive. I am less sure the BHZ gap is only awkward. Molenkamp's observation was guided by that HgTe prediction, so the citation wording should not say that Kane and Mele predicted the HgTe effect. I would word it around the Z2 quantum spin Hall state and its first observation, so that it stays accurate with the supplied names. I share your concern about the 2016 overlap, and I would like to hear whether you think it is a real obstacle or only a point for the citation text.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube (B008) first as a direct discovery from nature that opened neutrino astronomy, while admitting that single-name credit is a real question, and ranks B013 second.
responses.response: This was also my opening first choice, so I am sympathetic: the diffuse flux is confirmed in several channels and the blazar and Galactic-plane results are strong. My difficulty is the one you flag. A prize to Halzen alone, with AMANDA and the Baikal and ANTARES pioneers and the collaboration leadership outside the supplied credit, is hard to defend as a fair configuration. Source identification is also still partial. I would keep B008 as a live alternative, and if the committee can find a defensible multi-person credit, it could be a second part alongside another achievement. As the credit stands I do not think it can lead. Do you see a credible way to widen the credit within the three-name limit?

responses.point: Olsson ranks B013 first for its clear experimental footing, but ranks IceCube last of her shortlist entries (8) because a single credited name cannot represent the original work.
responses.response: I agree with you on the attribution problem for B008, and your doubt that a fair configuration can be reached from this credit is the main reason I have moved off it. Where I differ a little is on scientific standing. The discovery of the diffuse astrophysical flux is secure and I would not call it weak, so I would treat the issue as a credit problem, not a doubt about the physics. I also welcome your emphasis on experimental footing for B013. It supports using Molenkamp's HgTe transport result as the experimental anchor, though I note your concern that Hasan is left out.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B009) first as a mature, reproduced platform for strong light-matter coupling, while flagging that overlap with the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize and his own field bias may be an issue.
responses.response: I take your point that cQED is mature and that Wallraff and Schoelkopf's experiments are the basis of present quantum processors. My concern is timing and overlap: the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits is only a year old, and the committee would have to explain why the platform returns so soon. The credit set also leaves out Girvin, who co-authored the 2004 proposal, which makes a clean three-person split harder. I appreciate your flagging your closeness to the field, and I think that is the right thing to do. I would keep B009 outside my preferred configuration, while recognising it is a serious candidate.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts a Kane, Mele, Molenkamp trio that omits Hasan's three-dimensional topological insulator work and the BHZ proposers, and how the citation should be worded to be accurate about what each credited person did.
How strongly the 2016 prize on topological phases weighs against a second topological prize, and whether the difference in scope can be stated clearly.
Whether any multi-person credit for IceCube can be defended within the supplied names, since B008 is my scientifically preferred non-condensed-matter alternative.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for these candidates. My PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations and my KTH group are in astroparticle physics, and none of the people credited in B013, B025 or B008 is a known colleague or collaborator. I also note that I cannot be fully neutral on B008 because of my field.
